## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. **Describe** the monitoring-and-control loop and the performance measurement baseline.
2. **Read** the three earned-value curves: planned value (PV), earned value (EV), and actual cost (AC).
3. **Compute** schedule and cost variance and the SPI / CPI performance indices.
4. **Forecast** with EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI, and interpret them.
5. **Run** integrated change control so the baseline stays meaningful.
6. **Report** status honestly and recognize the "watermelon" trap.

<details>
<summary>Before we begin: the project has spent 60 % of its money --- is it 60 % done?</summary>

Almost certainly not. "Percent of budget spent" and "percent of work finished"
are different numbers, and the gap between them is the whole subject of this
chapter.

</details>

## Introduction: from a plan to a control system

You have planned the RC-vehicle project --- scope, WBS, schedule, budget. It is
now **week 8**. The sponsor asks the only question that matters at this stage:
**are we on track, and if not, how far off, and what will it cost to finish?**

Answering that needs a **control system**: a closed loop that **measures**
progress, **compares** it to the baseline, **analyzes** the variance, and drives
a corrective **action** --- then measures again.

```{r fig-control-loop-12, fig.cap="The monitoring-and-control loop. Without the 'compare to baseline' step, status reporting is just activity; with it, you get variance you can act on.", fig.align='center', fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
loop <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 2.2, 4.4, 6.6),
  y = 0,
  label = c("MEASURE\nprogress & cost", "COMPARE\nto baseline",
            "ANALYZE\nvariance", "ACT\ncorrective action")
)
ggplot(loop, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_label(aes(label = label), size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, lineheight = 0.9,
             fill = "#D6EAF8", linewidth = 0, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("segment", x = c(0.95, 3.15, 5.35), xend = c(1.55, 3.75, 5.95),
           y = 0, yend = 0, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), color = "grey40") +
  annotate("segment", x = 6.6, xend = 6.6, y = -0.17, yend = -0.5, color = "grey40") +
  annotate("segment", x = 6.6, xend = 0, y = -0.5, yend = -0.5, color = "grey40") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = -0.5, yend = -0.17,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.3, y = -0.5, label = "repeat every reporting period",
           size = 2.8 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "italic", color = "grey45",
           vjust = 1.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.9, 7.5), ylim = c(-0.75, 0.3)) +
  theme_void()
```

The reference for "compare" is the **performance measurement baseline** --- the
approved **scope + schedule + cost** locked in at the end of planning
([Chapter 9](09-Cost-Estimation-and-Budgeting.qmd)'s S-curve is its cost
dimension).

::: {.callout-note}
**Industry snapshot.** Earned value management is **contractually mandated** on
large U.S. defense programs (EIA-748). Automotive programs run a lighter version
at the milestone level. A food-plant capital project tracks committed vs. spent
vs. installed. The math below is the same at every scale.
:::

```{r video-evm-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
embed_youtube("x0EgZnXdunw", "What Is Earned Value? (Ricardo Vargas)")
```

## The three curves

Earned value management tracks three cumulative quantities against time:

| Term | Also called | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **PV** --- Planned Value | BCWS | The budgeted cost of the work **scheduled** to be done by now |
| **EV** --- Earned Value | BCWP | The budgeted cost of the work **actually done** by now |
| **AC** --- Actual Cost | ACWP | What has actually been **spent** to do that work |

**BAC** (Budget At Completion) is the total baseline budget --- where the PV curve
ends.

```{r fig-evm-curves-12, fig.cap="The three curves through week 8 of the RC-vehicle project (BAC = $620 000, off the top of this view). By the status date EV sits below PV -- behind schedule -- and AC sits above EV -- over cost. The vertical gaps at week 8 are the schedule and cost variances.", fig.align='center', fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
cutoff <- 8
wk <- seq(0, cutoff, by = 0.25)
# S-shaped ramps scaled to pass through the week-8 values in Worked Example 1.
shape <- function(t, k) (t / cutoff)^k
df <- data.frame(
  wk = wk,
  PV = 217000 * shape(wk, 1.8),
  EV = 186000 * shape(wk, 2.0),
  AC = 210000 * shape(wk, 1.7)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = df, aes(wk, PV, color = "PV (planned value)"), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = df, aes(wk, EV, color = "EV (earned value)"), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = df, aes(wk, AC, color = "AC (actual cost)"), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutoff, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(m = c("PV", "EV", "AC"), y = c(217000, 186000, 210000)),
             aes(x = cutoff, y = y, color = m), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = cutoff + 0.12, y = 228000, hjust = 0,
           label = "PV  $217 000", size = 3 * chart_text_scale, color = "#2E86C1") +
  annotate("text", x = cutoff + 0.12, y = 205000, hjust = 0,
           label = "AC  $210 000", size = 3 * chart_text_scale, color = "#C0392B") +
  annotate("text", x = cutoff + 0.12, y = 178000, hjust = 0,
           label = "EV  $186 000", size = 3 * chart_text_scale, color = "#27AE60") +
  annotate("text", x = cutoff - 0.25, y = 45000, hjust = 1,
           label = "status date\n(week 8)", size = 3 * chart_text_scale, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("PV (planned value)" = "#2E86C1",
                                "EV (earned value)" = "#27AE60",
                                "AC (actual cost)" = "#C0392B",
                                "PV" = "#2E86C1", "EV" = "#27AE60", "AC" = "#C0392B"),
                     breaks = c("PV (planned value)", "EV (earned value)", "AC (actual cost)"),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(big.mark = " ")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 9.7)) +
  labs(title = "Earned value: planned vs. earned vs. actual",
       x = "Project week", y = "Cumulative cost") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * chart_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * chart_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * chart_text_scale)
  )
```

## The six core metrics

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Schedule Variance} \quad SV &= EV - PV \\
\text{Cost Variance} \quad CV &= EV - AC \\
\text{Schedule Performance Index} \quad SPI &= EV / PV \\
\text{Cost Performance Index} \quad CPI &= EV / AC
\end{aligned}
$$

| Reading | Schedule | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Ahead / under** | $SV > 0$, $SPI > 1$ | $CV > 0$, $CPI > 1$ |
| **On plan** | $SV = 0$, $SPI = 1$ | $CV = 0$, $CPI = 1$ |
| **Behind / over** | $SV < 0$, $SPI < 1$ | $CV < 0$, $CPI < 1$ |

### Worked Example 1: the RC-vehicle project at week 8

Baseline budget **BAC = \$620 000**. By week 8 the plan said **35 %** of the
work should be done; **30 %** is actually done; **\$210 000** has been spent.

Live cell --- change the planned %, the actual %, or the actual cost.

```{r calc-evm-example-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
qwebr_calc_card(
  label = "evm-example-12",
  title = "Earned Value Calculator",
  icon = "chart-line",
  mode = "demo",
  inputs = list(
    qwebr_calc_input("BAC", "Budget at completion (BAC)", value = 620000, min = 200000, max = 1000000, step = 10000, type = "slider", prefix = "$"),
    qwebr_calc_input("planned_pct", "Planned % complete", value = 0.35, min = 0.05, max = 1, step = 0.01, type = "slider"),
    qwebr_calc_input("actual_pct", "Actual % complete", value = 0.3, min = 0, max = 1, step = 0.01, type = "slider"),
    qwebr_calc_input("AC", "Actual cost to date (AC)", value = 210000, min = 10000, max = 1000000, step = 5000, type = "slider", prefix = "$")
  )
)
```

<details class="qwebr-calc-source">
<summary>Show the live R code behind this calculator</summary>

The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further.

```{webr-r}
#| label: evm-example-12
BAC <- 620000
planned_pct <- 0.35
actual_pct  <- 0.30
AC <- 210000

PV <- planned_pct * BAC
EV <- actual_pct  * BAC

SV  <- EV - PV
CV  <- EV - AC
SPI <- EV / PV
CPI <- EV / AC

money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))

par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1)
bp <- barplot(c(PV, EV, AC) / 1000, names.arg = c("PV", "EV", "AC"), col = c("#bdc3c7", "#16a085", ifelse(AC > EV, "#e74c3c", "#2980b9")),
              ylim = c(0, 1100), ylab = "$ thousand",
              main = "Planned vs. earned vs. actual")

sched <- if (SV < 0) "!!behind schedule!!" else "on or ahead of schedule"
cost  <- if (CV < 0) "!!over budget!!" else "on or under budget"
cat(sprintf("Project is %s and %s\n", sched, cost))
cat(sprintf("Planned value (PV)  %s\n", money(PV)))
cat(sprintf("Earned value (EV)  %s\n", money(EV)))
cat(sprintf("Actual cost (AC)  %s\n", money(AC)))
cat(sprintf("Schedule variance (SV)  %s\n", money(SV)))
cat(sprintf("Cost variance (CV)  %s\n", money(CV)))
cat(sprintf("SPI  %.3f (%.0f cents of schedule per planned dollar)\n", SPI, SPI * 100))
cat(sprintf("CPI  %.3f (%.0f cents of work per dollar spent)\n", CPI, CPI * 100))
```

</details>

The project is **behind schedule and over cost** --- and this is visible in week 8,
while there is still time to act, instead of as a surprise at the end.

## PV, EV and AC are running totals from day 0

The three numbers in Worked Example 1 are not "this week's" numbers, and they
are not the numbers for one task. Each one is a **running total for the whole
project, from the first day up to the status date**:

- **PV** adds up the budget of *all* the work the plan said would be done
  between week 0 and the status date --- including work packages that were
  planned to finish weeks ago.
- **EV** adds up the budget value of *all* the work actually completed since
  week 0, finished packages included.
- **AC** adds up *all* the money actually spent since week 0.

A work package that finished in week 2 still counts in PV, EV and AC at week
8. That is why the curves in the figure above only ever go up.

The project's **SPI** and **CPI** are then the ratios of those project totals:
$SPI = \sum EV / \sum PV$ and $CPI = \sum EV / \sum AC$. You may work out the
variance of each work package to find *where* the trouble is, but the project
status always comes from the totals.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Common mistake: averaging the task indices.** Never work out a CPI or SPI for
each task and then average them. An average treats a \$4 000 decal job the
same as a \$250 000 tooling package, and a task that has only just started
(EV still 0) drags the average towards zero. The project CPI weights every
task by its dollars automatically, because it divides the totals.
:::

```{r tbl-evm-average-trap-12, echo=FALSE}
trap <- data.frame(Package = c("Tooling", "Labels and decals"),
                   EV = c(200000, 6000), AC = c(250000, 4000))
trap$CPI <- trap$EV / trap$AC
avg_cpi <- mean(trap$CPI)
prj_cpi <- sum(trap$EV) / sum(trap$AC)
trap_show <- rbind(
  data.frame(Package = trap$Package,
             `EV ($)` = format(trap$EV, big.mark = " "), `AC ($)` = format(trap$AC, big.mark = " "),
             CPI = sprintf("%.2f", trap$CPI), check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Package = "WRONG: average of the two CPIs", `EV ($)` = "", `AC ($)` = "",
             CPI = sprintf("%.2f  (looks under budget)", avg_cpi), check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Package = "RIGHT: project totals", `EV ($)` = format(sum(trap$EV), big.mark = " "),
             `AC ($)` = format(sum(trap$AC), big.mark = " "),
             CPI = sprintf("%.2f  (over budget)", prj_cpi), check.names = FALSE))
knitr::kable(trap_show, align = c("l", "r", "r", "l"),
             caption = "Averaging task CPIs hides an overrun. The project CPI comes from the totals.") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  kableExtra::row_spec(3, color = "#C0392B") |>
  kableExtra::row_spec(4, bold = TRUE, color = "#186A3B")
```

The average says the project earns \$1.15 of work for every dollar spent. In
fact it earns only `r sprintf("%.2f", prj_cpi)`: about
`r round(100 * (1 - prj_cpi))` cents of every dollar spent so far bought no
work.

### Class exercise: PV, EV and AC from the time-phased plan

This exercise builds the three numbers from scratch, the way a project control
system does. A four-package project has a **time-phased budget**: the planned
spend of each work package in each week (the S-curve data from
[Chapter 9](09-Cost-Estimation-and-Budgeting.qmd)). The status date is the
**end of week 6**.

**What to do.**

1. In the first table, add across each row to get the **planned spend for that
   week**, then keep a **running total** from week 1. The running total at
   the status date is the project's **PV**.
2. In the second table, find each package's **PV to the end of week 6** (the
   sum of its planned spend in weeks 1 to 6) and check that the four add up to
   the PV from step 1. Then find each package's **EV = BAC x % complete**.
   The actual costs are given: they are everything booked to each package
   since week 1.
3. Add each column for the **project totals**, then compute the project SPI,
   CPI and EAC from those totals.

**What it means.** Design finished in week 4, but its full budget still
counts in PV, EV and AC at week 6: completed work never drops out of the
totals. Assembly was planned to start in week 6 and has not started, so it
adds to PV but nothing to EV --- that is part of why the project is behind.

```{r tryit-evm-timephased-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
tp_pkgs <- c("Design", "Tooling", "Assembly", "Testing")
tp_plan_table <- function(m) {
  d <- data.frame(Week = 1:10)
  for (i in seq_along(tp_pkgs)) d[[paste0(tp_pkgs[i], " ($)")]] <- m[i, ]
  d[["Planned this week ($)"]] <- colSums(m)
  d[["Cumulative PV ($)"]] <- cumsum(colSums(m))
  d
}
tp_status_table <- function(m, wk, pct, ac) {
  bac <- rowSums(m)
  d <- data.frame(`Work package` = tp_pkgs, `BAC ($)` = bac, check.names = FALSE)
  d[[sprintf("PV to end of week %d ($)", wk)]] <- rowSums(m[, 1:wk, drop = FALSE])
  d[["Complete %"]] <- pct
  d[["EV ($)"]] <- bac * pct / 100
  d[[sprintf("AC to end of week %d ($)", wk)]] <- ac
  d
}
tp_answers <- function(m, wk, pct, ac) {
  pv <- sum(m[, 1:wk]); ev <- sum(rowSums(m) * pct / 100); a <- sum(ac)
  list(tryit_answer(sprintf("Project PV at the end of week %d", wk), pv, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project EV", ev, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project AC", a, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project SPI = total EV / total PV", ev / pv, tol = 0.005),
       tryit_answer("Project CPI = total EV / total AC", ev / a, tol = 0.005),
       tryit_answer("EAC = BAC / CPI", sum(m) / (ev / a), tol = 1, tol_pct = 0.2, prefix = "$"))
}
tp_hints_plan <- c(`Planned this week ($)` = "Add the four packages' planned spend for that week.",
                   `Cumulative PV ($)` = "Running total from week 1: this week's plan plus last week's cumulative PV.")

# Class data set: status at the end of week 6.
tp_m <- rbind(c(rep(10, 4), rep(0, 6)),          # Design, weeks 1-4
              c(0, 0, rep(15, 6), 0, 0),         # Tooling, weeks 3-8
              c(rep(0, 5), rep(12, 4), 0),       # Assembly, weeks 6-9
              c(rep(0, 7), 6, 8, 8)) * 1000      # Testing, weeks 8-10
tp_wk <- 6; tp_pct <- c(100, 55, 0, 0); tp_ac <- c(44000, 58000, 0, 0)

tryit_grid(
  "evm-timephased-plan", "Step 1: the time-phased budget and cumulative PV",
  data = tp_plan_table(tp_m), blank = c("Planned this week ($)", "Cumulative PV ($)"),
  tol = 1, digits = 0, hints = tp_hints_plan,
  answers = list(tryit_answer("PV at the end of week 6", sum(tp_m[, 1:tp_wk]), tol = 1, prefix = "$")),
  intro = "Planned spend in dollars for each package in each week. The status date is the end of week 6.")

tryit_grid(
  "evm-timephased-status", "Step 2: PV, EV and AC by package, then the project status",
  data = tp_status_table(tp_m, tp_wk, tp_pct, tp_ac),
  blank = c("PV to end of week 6 ($)", "EV ($)"), tol = 1, digits = 0,
  hints = c(`PV to end of week 6 ($)` = "Add that package's planned spend for weeks 1 to 6 in the first table.",
            `EV ($)` = "BAC x % complete."),
  answers = tp_answers(tp_m, tp_wk, tp_pct, tp_ac),
  intro = "Status at the end of week 6. SPI and CPI come from the project totals, never from averaging the packages.")

# Graded twin: a different plan, status at the end of week 5.
tw_m <- rbind(c(rep(10, 3), rep(0, 7)),          # Design, weeks 1-3
              c(0, rep(20, 6), 0, 0, 0),         # Tooling, weeks 2-7
              c(rep(0, 4), rep(15, 4), 0, 0),    # Assembly, weeks 5-8
              c(rep(0, 7), 10, 10, 10)) * 1000   # Testing, weeks 8-10
tw_wk <- 5; tw_pct <- c(100, 60, 10, 0); tw_ac <- c(32000, 75000, 9000, 0)
tryit_grid(
  "evm-timephased-twin", "PV, EV and AC from a time-phased budget (graded)", show = FALSE,
  data = tp_plan_table(tw_m), blank = c("Planned this week ($)", "Cumulative PV ($)"),
  tol = 1, digits = 0,
  answers = tp_answers(tw_m, tw_wk, tw_pct, tw_ac),
  question = paste0("<p>A project has four work packages with the planned spend per week shown ",
    "(dollars). The status date is the end of week 5. At that date Design is 100 % complete, ",
    "Tooling 60 %, Assembly 10 % and Testing 0 %. The actual costs booked since week 1 are ",
    "Design $32 000, Tooling $75 000, Assembly $9 000 and Testing $0. Complete the weekly and ",
    "cumulative planned spend, then give the project PV, EV and AC at the end of week 5, the ",
    "project SPI and CPI (three decimals, from the project totals) and the EAC = BAC / CPI.</p>"))
```

<details class="tryit-solution">
<summary>Show the worked solution</summary>

**Step 1.** The weekly planned spend is \$10 000, \$10 000, \$25 000,
\$25 000, \$15 000, \$27 000, \$27 000, \$33 000, \$20 000 and \$8 000. The
running total is \$10 000, \$20 000, \$45 000, \$70 000, \$85 000,
**\$112 000**, \$139 000, \$172 000, \$192 000 and \$200 000 (the BAC). PV at
the end of week 6 is **\$112 000**.

**Step 2.** PV by package to the end of week 6: Design \$40 000 (all four of
its weeks), Tooling \$60 000 (weeks 3 to 6), Assembly \$12 000 (week 6),
Testing \$0. They add up to the same \$112 000. EV: Design 100 % of \$40 000
= \$40 000, Tooling 55 % of \$90 000 = \$49 500, Assembly and Testing \$0, so
EV = **\$89 500**. AC = \$44 000 + \$58 000 = **\$102 000**.

**Project status.** SPI = 89 500 / 112 000 = **0.799** (behind schedule),
CPI = 89 500 / 102 000 = **0.877** (over cost), and EAC = 200 000 / 0.877 =
**about \$227 900**. Assembly has not started on time: it carries \$12 000 of
PV and no EV, and that is a schedule warning even though it has cost nothing
yet.

</details>

### Try it yourself: earned value by work package

Each work package has its budget, how much of it was planned to be done **by
now, counting from the start of the project**, how much is actually done, and
everything it has cost since the start. Design was planned to finish weeks
ago, so its whole budget is in PV. Work out PV, EV, CV and SV for each
package, add the columns to get the **project totals**, and only then compute
the project SPI, CPI and forecast from those totals. Each team picks its own
**data set**.

```{r tryit-evm-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
ev_names <- c("Design", "Tooling", "Assembly", "Testing")
# Every set has BAC = $620 000, as in Worked Example 1. "Planned %" and "AC" are
# cumulative from the start of the project, so finished packages carry their
# whole budget in PV.
ev_sets <- list(
  data.frame(bac = c(120000, 260000, 150000, 90000), plan = c(100, 90, 40, 10), done = c(100, 70, 30, 0), ac = c(126000, 205000, 52000, 3000)),
  data.frame(bac = c(150000, 220000, 160000, 90000), plan = c(100, 80, 35, 5), done = c(100, 85, 25, 0), ac = c(148000, 196000, 45000, 2000)),
  data.frame(bac = c(100000, 280000, 170000, 70000), plan = c(100, 100, 50, 20), done = c(100, 90, 55, 15), ac = c(97000, 262000, 90000, 9000)),
  data.frame(bac = c(130000, 240000, 180000, 70000), plan = c(100, 75, 30, 0), done = c(95, 80, 20, 0), ac = c(140000, 185000, 40000, 0)))
ev_table <- function(s) {
  pv <- s$bac * s$plan / 100; ev <- s$bac * s$done / 100
  data.frame(`Work package` = ev_names, `BAC ($)` = s$bac, `Planned % to date` = s$plan,
             `Complete % to date` = s$done, `AC to date ($)` = s$ac, `PV to date ($)` = pv,
             `EV to date ($)` = ev, `CV ($)` = ev - s$ac, `SV ($)` = ev - pv, check.names = FALSE)
}
ev_answers <- function(s) {
  t <- ev_table(s); bac <- sum(s$bac); pv <- sum(t$`PV to date ($)`); ev <- sum(t$`EV to date ($)`); ac <- sum(s$ac)
  list(tryit_answer("Project PV (all packages, since the start)", pv, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project EV (all packages, since the start)", ev, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project AC (all packages, since the start)", ac, tol = 1, prefix = "$"),
       tryit_answer("Project SPI = total EV / total PV", ev / pv, tol = 0.005),
       tryit_answer("Project CPI = total EV / total AC", ev / ac, tol = 0.005),
       tryit_answer("EAC = BAC / CPI", bac / (ev / ac), tol = 1, tol_pct = 0.2, prefix = "$"))
}
ev_cols <- c("PV to date ($)", "EV to date ($)", "CV ($)", "SV ($)")
tryit_grid(
  "evm-by-package", "Earned value by work package",
  data = ev_table(ev_sets[[1]]), blank = ev_cols, tol = 1, digits = 0,
  answers = ev_answers(ev_sets[[1]]),
  teams = lapply(ev_sets[-1], function(s) list(data = ev_table(s), answers = ev_answers(s))),
  hints = c(`PV to date ($)` = "BAC x planned % to date: everything this package should have done since the project began.",
            `EV to date ($)` = "BAC x complete % to date.",
            `CV ($)` = "EV - AC.", `SV ($)` = "EV - PV."),
  intro = "Add up PV, EV and AC over all four packages first. SPI and CPI come from those totals, never from averaging the packages. Three decimals for the indices.")

ev_twin <- data.frame(bac = c(140000, 250000, 150000, 80000), plan = c(100, 85, 40, 0),
                      done = c(100, 75, 35, 5), ac = c(135000, 200000, 58000, 4000))
tryit_grid(
  "evm-twin", "Earned value by work package (graded)", show = FALSE,
  data = ev_table(ev_twin), blank = ev_cols, tol = 1, digits = 0, answers = ev_answers(ev_twin),
  question = paste0("<p>A project has four work packages with the budget (BAC), planned % complete, ",
    "actual % complete and actual cost (AC), all counted from the start of the project. For each package ",
    "calculate PV, EV, CV and SV. Then give the project totals of PV, EV and AC, the project SPI and CPI ",
    "from those totals (three decimals), and the estimate at completion BAC / CPI.</p>"))
```

<details class="tryit-solution">
<summary>Show the worked solution</summary>

PV = BAC x planned %, EV = BAC x actual %, CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV, all
counted from the start of the project. For data set 1 the project totals are
BAC \$620 000, PV **\$423 000**, EV **\$347 000** and AC **\$386 000**, so
SPI = 347 / 423 = **0.820**, CPI = 347 / 386 = **0.899** and EAC = 620 000 /
0.899 = **about \$689 700**. Design finished long ago, yet its full
\$120 000 is still in PV, EV and AC. Tooling is the package doing the damage:
it is both behind (SV = -\$52 000) and over (CV = -\$23 000).

Now try the wrong way. The four package CPIs are 0.952, 0.888, 0.865 and 0
(Testing has spent \$3 000 and earned nothing yet). Their average is 0.676,
which says the project is losing a third of every dollar. It is not: weighted
by the dollars, the true project CPI is 0.899. In data set 3 the trap runs the
other way: the package CPIs average 1.05 ("under budget") while the project
CPI is 0.996. Always divide the totals.

</details>

## Forecasting

| Forecast | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **EAC** (Estimate At Completion) | $BAC / CPI$ | Total cost if current cost efficiency holds |
| EAC (schedule too) | $AC + \dfrac{BAC - EV}{CPI \times SPI}$ | If both cost *and* schedule performance persist |
| EAC (one-off overrun) | $AC + (BAC - EV)$ | If the overrun so far was a one-time event |
| **ETC** (Estimate To Complete) | $EAC - AC$ | Money still needed from here |
| **VAC** (Variance At Completion) | $BAC - EAC$ | Projected total over/under budget |
| **TCPI** (To-Complete Performance Index) | $\dfrac{BAC - EV}{BAC - AC}$ | The cost efficiency the *remaining* work must hit to still land on BAC |

### Try it yourself: EAC scenarios

```{r calc-eac-scenarios-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
qwebr_calc_card(
  label = "eac-scenarios-12",
  title = "Estimate-at-Completion Scenarios",
  icon = "forward",
  mode = "task",
  inputs = list(
    qwebr_calc_input("BAC", "Budget at completion (BAC)", value = 620000, min = 100000, max = 2000000, step = 10000, prefix = "$"),
    qwebr_calc_input("EV", "Earned value (EV)", value = 186000, min = 1000, max = 2000000, step = 1000, prefix = "$"),
    qwebr_calc_input("AC", "Actual cost (AC)", value = 210000, min = 1000, max = 2000000, step = 1000, prefix = "$"),
    qwebr_calc_input("PV", "Planned value (PV)", value = 217000, min = 1000, max = 2000000, step = 1000, prefix = "$")
  ),
  goal = "Find the actual cost to date at which the original budget is still achievable (TCPI of 1 or less).",
  goal_test = "tcpi <= 1"
)
```

<details class="qwebr-calc-source">
<summary>Show the live R code behind this calculator</summary>

The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further.

```{webr-r}
#| label: eac-scenarios-12
BAC <- 620000
EV  <- 186000
AC  <- 210000
PV  <- 217000
CPI <- EV / AC
SPI <- EV / PV

eac_cpi       <- BAC / CPI
eac_oneoff    <- AC + (BAC - EV)
eac_cost_sched<- AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI * SPI)

etc  <- eac_cpi - AC
vac  <- BAC - eac_cpi
tcpi <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC)

money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))

eacs <- c("BAC\n(plan)" = BAC, "CPI\ncontinues" = eac_cpi, "One-off\noverrun" = eac_oneoff,
          "Cost and\nschedule" = eac_cost_sched)
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1)
barplot(eacs / 1000, col = c("#bdc3c7", "#2980b9", "#16a085", "#8e44ad"),
        ylim = c(0, max(eacs) / 1000 * 1.1), ylab = "$ thousand", main = "Estimate at completion by scenario")
abline(h = BAC / 1000, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#e74c3c")

msg <- if (tcpi > 1.10) {
  "!!a big ask; the BAC is likely unrealistic now!!"
} else if (tcpi > 1.0) {
  "recoverable, but the team must run leaner than planned"
} else {
  "achievable"
}
cat(sprintf("TCPI %.3f: %s\n", tcpi, msg))
cat(sprintf("CPI  %.3f\n", CPI))
cat(sprintf("SPI  %.3f\n", SPI))
cat(sprintf("EAC, cost efficiency continues  %s\n", money(eac_cpi)))
cat(sprintf("EAC, overrun was a one-off  %s\n", money(eac_oneoff)))
cat(sprintf("EAC, cost AND schedule persist  %s\n", money(eac_cost_sched)))
cat(sprintf("ETC (money still needed)  %s\n", money(etc)))
cat(sprintf("VAC (projected overrun)  %s\n", money(vac)))
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Which EAC formula should you actually report?</summary>

It depends on *why* you are over. If a one-time event caused it (a failed test
you have since fixed), $AC + (BAC - EV)$ is fair. If the overrun reflects how the
team is fundamentally working (rates, productivity), $BAC/CPI$ is the honest
number. If you are *also* behind schedule and recovery will cost overtime, the
$CPI \times SPI$ version is the most conservative. Report the one your evidence
supports --- and say which assumption you made.

</details>

### Try it yourself: which forecast do you report?

```{r tryit-eac-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
eac_bins <- c("BAC / CPI (efficiency continues)", "AC + (BAC - EV) (one-off overrun)",
              "AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) (cost and schedule persist)")
tryit_sort(
  "eac-formula", "Which EAC formula does each situation call for?",
  bins = eac_bins,
  cards = data.frame(
    text = c("A one-off equipment failure caused the overrun and it has been repaired.",
             "The overrun reflects how this team works: its rates and productivity will not change.",
             "The project is over cost and behind schedule, and catching up will need overtime.",
             "A single failed test cost $30 000 and will not happen again.",
             "The cost efficiency so far is typical of this team.",
             "The slip must be recovered with premium-rate crews, so both indices will persist."),
    bin = c(eac_bins[2], eac_bins[1], eac_bins[3], eac_bins[2], eac_bins[1], eac_bins[3]),
    why = c("A one-off: assume the rest of the work goes to budget.",
            "The fundamentals persist: BAC / CPI is the honest number.",
            "Both cost and schedule performance persist: the most conservative.",
            "A one-time event: add the remaining budgeted work to AC.",
            "Cost efficiency continues: BAC / CPI.", "Both indices persist: the conservative formula."),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  intro = "Report the formula your evidence supports.", question = NULL)

tryit_sort(
  "eac-formula-twin", "EAC formula (graded)", bins = eac_bins, show = FALSE,
  cards = data.frame(
    text = c("A supplier's late delivery cost $12 000 once and is resolved.",
             "The new line is simply slower than planned, and will stay that way.",
             "Behind schedule and over budget, with overtime planned to recover."),
    bin = c(eac_bins[2], eac_bins[1], eac_bins[3]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  question = "<p>For each situation, choose the estimate-at-completion formula that matches the assumption.</p>")
```

## Reading the S-curve honestly

- **Spend is not progress.** A project can be on budget (AC ≈ PV) and badly behind (EV ≪ PV) --- it just has not done the work yet.
- **The "watermelon" report** --- green on the outside, red on the inside. High-level status shows green because spend matches plan, while the earned value underneath is red.
- **Leading vs. lagging indicators.** SPI and CPI are somewhat lagging. Leading signals --- rising defect find-rate, slipping sub-milestones, key staff leaving --- warn you earlier. Watch both.

### Try it yourself: read the status

```{r tryit-status-12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
st_bins <- c("Ahead and under budget", "Behind but under budget", "Ahead but over budget", "Behind and over budget")
tryit_sort(
  "status-quadrant", "What is each project's real condition?",
  bins = st_bins,
  cards = data.frame(
    text = c("SPI 1.10, CPI 1.05", "SPI 0.85, CPI 1.10", "SPI 1.12, CPI 0.90", "SPI 0.80, CPI 0.92",
             "PV $300k, EV $270k, AC $250k", "PV $200k, EV $230k, AC $260k",
             "PV $400k, EV $380k, AC $410k", "PV $150k, EV $165k, AC $150k"),
    bin = c(st_bins[1], st_bins[2], st_bins[3], st_bins[4], st_bins[2], st_bins[3], st_bins[4], st_bins[1]),
    why = c("Both indices above 1.", "SPI below 1 (behind), CPI above 1 (under budget).",
            "SPI above 1, CPI below 1.", "Both below 1.",
            "SPI = 270/300 = 0.90, CPI = 270/250 = 1.08.", "SPI = 230/200 = 1.15, CPI = 230/260 = 0.88.",
            "SPI = 380/400 = 0.95, CPI = 380/410 = 0.93.", "SPI = 165/150 = 1.10, CPI = 165/150 = 1.10."),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  intro = "An index above 1 is good. Work out SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC where needed.", question = NULL)

tryit_sort(
  "status-quadrant-twin", "Project status (graded)", bins = st_bins, show = FALSE,
  cards = data.frame(
    text = c("PV $500k, EV $450k, AC $430k", "PV $250k, EV $275k, AC $240k", "SPI 1.08, CPI 0.88",
             "SPI 0.90, CPI 0.85"),
    bin = c(st_bins[2], st_bins[1], st_bins[3], st_bins[4]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  question = "<p>For each project (SPI = EV/PV, CPI = EV/AC), choose its condition.</p>")
```

## Integrated change control

Control only works against a **meaningful baseline**. Every change request goes
through the same gate as in [Chapter 3](03-Scope-and-Organizational-Structures.qmd):
assess the impact on scope, schedule, and cost; approve or reject; and if
approved, **re-baseline** so future variance is measured against the new plan ---
not the old one you can no longer hit. **Configuration management** keeps the
product definition (drawings, specs, software versions) in step with the
approved baseline.

## Status reporting

On a real project the reporting instruments are the periodic **status report**
and the **dashboard**: they roll up progress, cost, schedule, risks, and issues
on a fixed cadence. Good reporting is **honest** (report the red while it
is still fixable), **consistent** (same metrics every period so trends are
visible), and **actionable** (every variance has an owner and a next step). A
dashboard that only ever shows green is not a control system --- it is a
comfort blanket.

## Key Takeaways

- **Control** is a closed loop: **measure → compare to baseline → analyze variance → act**, every reporting period.
- Track **PV** (work scheduled), **EV** (work done), **AC** (money spent), all in budget dollars, against **BAC**.
- $SV = EV - PV$, $CV = EV - AC$, $SPI = EV/PV$, $CPI = EV/AC$. Below 1 / negative = behind / over.
- Forecast with **EAC** ($BAC/CPI$ is the common honest form), **ETC** $= EAC - AC$, **VAC** $= BAC - EAC$, **TCPI** $= (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC)$.
- **Spend is not progress.** Beware the **watermelon** report; watch **leading** indicators, not just SPI/CPI.
- Keep the **baseline meaningful** through integrated change control and configuration management.
- Report **honestly, consistently, and actionably** --- every variance gets an owner.

## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 12

::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 12: One Good Number Doesn't Make a Good Week"}

Day 50, and it's time to run the loop this chapter just walked you through
--- measure, compare, analyze, act --- against real Trailblazer numbers
instead of a textbook example. Sofia Reyes's weekly report lands with a
summary line that looks encouraging at a glance: spend is roughly tracking
the plan. You know better than to stop at a glance.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| BAC (Budget At Completion) | \$761,300 |
| PV (Planned Value, day 50) | \$560,000 |
| EV (Earned Value, day 50) | \$520,000 |
| AC (Actual Cost, day 50) | \$545,000 |

You run the four core numbers yourself before the steering call. CV = EV −
AC = \$520,000 − \$545,000 = **−\$25,000** --- over budget. SV = EV − PV =
\$520,000 − \$560,000 = **−\$40,000** --- behind schedule. CPI = EV/AC =
520/545 ≈ **0.95**. SPI = EV/PV = 520/560 ≈ **0.93**. Running BAC/CPI forward
gives an EAC of roughly **\$798,000** --- a forecast, not a certainty, but not
a comfortable one either.

The schedule slip traces to one place: activity H, toy-safety certification,
which has sat on the critical path with zero float since the CPM network was
first built back in Week 6. The certification lab pushed back its review
date, and because H has no float, every day it slips is a day the whole
67-day project finish slips with it.

The cost story is the sharper lesson. Two weeks ago, you talked MCS down
from \$145,000 to **\$136,000** for the motor-and-controller package
--- a genuine \$9,000 win, hard-negotiated, real money, and the whole point
of using the competing Paragon quote as leverage. So why is AC still running
\$25,000 ahead of EV? Because elsewhere on the project, packaging samples had
to move by expedited freight to protect the schedule, and that bill quietly
ate the MCS saving and then some. A favourable variance on one activity,
read on its own, told the team nothing reliable about the project's overall
health --- exactly the trap this chapter's "watermelon" warning describes:
green on the outside, red once you look underneath.

There is a sliver of good news buried in the bad. At roughly \$798,000, the
EAC still sits just under Daniel Cho's \$800,000 charter ceiling from Week 3
--- a thin margin, but a margin, assuming nothing else slips before Week
13's closeout.

:::

## Practice Problems

<details>
<summary>Problem 1: Full EVM snapshot</summary>

BAC = \$400 000. At the status date: PV = \$180 000, EV = \$150 000,
AC = \$165 000. Compute SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC (BAC/CPI), ETC, VAC, TCPI, and
state the project's condition in one sentence.

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```{r p1-evm-12, echo=TRUE}
BAC <- 400000; PV <- 180000; EV <- 150000; AC <- 165000
SV <- EV - PV; CV <- EV - AC; SPI <- EV / PV; CPI <- EV / AC
EAC <- BAC / CPI; ETC <- EAC - AC; VAC <- BAC - EAC
TCPI <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC)
cat(sprintf("SV=$%s  CV=$%s  SPI=%.3f  CPI=%.3f\n",
            format(SV, big.mark=" "), format(CV, big.mark=" "), SPI, CPI))
cat(sprintf("EAC=$%s  ETC=$%s  VAC=$%s  TCPI=%.3f\n",
            format(round(EAC), big.mark=" "), format(round(ETC), big.mark=" "),
            format(round(VAC), big.mark=" "), TCPI))
```

Behind schedule (SPI 0.83) and over cost (CPI 0.91); projected to finish about
\$40 000 over budget, and the remaining work must run at TCPI ≈ 1.06 to still
hit BAC.

</details>

</details>

<details>
<summary>Problem 2: On budget but in trouble</summary>

A project reports PV = \$500 000, EV = \$400 000, AC = \$400 000. The sponsor
sees "spend exactly matches earned value --- CPI = 1.0 --- we're fine." Are they?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Cost efficiency is fine (CPI = 1.0), but **SPI = EV/PV = 0.80** ---
the project has completed only 80 % of the work it should have by now. It is
**20 % behind schedule** and will either finish late or need to spend more
(overtime, added staff) to catch up, which will then push CPI below 1. This is
the classic watermelon: the cost view is green, the schedule view is red.

</details>

</details>

<details>
<summary>Problem 3 (discussion): re-baseline or not?</summary>

At week 8 the RC-vehicle project is forecast (EAC) at \$700 000 against a
\$620 000 BAC, mostly because the retailer added a second body colourway
(an approved scope change) and the new line's learning curve ran longer than
planned. Should you re-baseline?

<details>
<summary>Discussion points</summary>

Split the two causes. The **approved scope change** is a
legitimate reason to re-baseline --- the extra colourway was authorised, so the
budget and schedule should be formally updated and future variance measured
against the new plan. The **learning-curve overrun** is *performance* against
the plan, not a change to the plan --- that stays as variance you must recover or
explain. Re-baselining to bury performance problems ("we'll just move the
goalposts") destroys the value of the control system; re-baselining for
authorised changes keeps it honest.

</details>

</details>
